crater: A round hole in the ground made by a falling meteorite or by a volcano. The Moon is covered in them.
heliocentrism: The idea that the Sun is at the centre, and the Earth and the other planets go around it.
science fiction: Stories that imagine the future, space travel or amazing inventions, based on science.
rocket: A machine that moves forward by throwing very hot gases out backwards. It is the only way to reach space, because it works even without air.
action and reaction: A law discovered by Newton: when you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard, in the opposite direction.
stage: A section of a rocket with its own engines and fuel tanks. When it is empty, it drops off to make the rocket lighter.
missile: A rocket that carries a bomb. The first big rockets were built as missiles.
cold war: The long rivalry (1947–1991) between the United States and the Soviet Union, who opposed each other without fighting a war directly.
orbit: The circular or oval path that an object follows as it goes around a planet or star, like the Moon around the Earth.
satellite: An object that goes around a planet. The Moon is a natural satellite; artificial satellites are built by people.
weightlessness: The feeling of weighing nothing that astronauts have in orbit: everything floats, both objects and people.
space agency: An organisation set up by one or more countries to plan and carry out space missions, like NASA, CNES or ESA.
space probe: A machine with nobody on board, sent to explore the Moon, planets or comets and controlled from Earth.
cosmonaut: A space traveller, especially from Russia. The word comes from the Greek "kosmos" (universe) and "nautes" (sailor).
astronaut: A space traveller. The word comes from the Greek "astron" (star) and "nautes" (sailor): a star sailor!
atmosphere: The layer of air around a planet. It lets us breathe and protects us, but it heats up spacecraft coming back into it enormously.
segregation: Keeping people apart because of the colour of their skin, with different schools, places or rights. It was the law in the southern United States.
spacewalk: When an astronaut goes outside their spacecraft or station and floats in space in a spacesuit.
equator: The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the North Pole and the South Pole.
environment: The natural world around us: air, water, soil, plants and animals. Protecting it means taking care of the planet.
lunar module: The small Apollo spacecraft that flew down from orbit to the Moon's surface, then back up, with two astronauts.
gravity: The force that pulls things towards each other. It makes us fall to the ground and keeps the Moon going around the Earth.
space station: A large home orbiting the Earth, where astronauts live and work for weeks or months.
greenhouse effect: When some gases in the atmosphere trap the Sun's heat, like the glass of a greenhouse. Too much of it warms a planet.
interstellar: Between the stars, far beyond the planets of the Solar System.
telecommunications: Ways of communicating at a distance: telephone, television, radio, the Internet.
space shuttle: A reusable American spacecraft (1981–2011) that took off like a rocket and landed like a plane.
spationaute: A French word for space travellers, used especially for those from France and Europe.
module: A section of a space station, launched separately and then joined to the others in space, like a piece of a construction set.
universe: Everything that exists: planets, stars, galaxies, space and time. It is thought to have begun about 13.8 billion years ago.
black hole: A place in space where matter is squeezed so tightly that its gravity pulls in everything, even light, which can't get out.
light-year: The distance light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion kilometres! It is used to measure how far away stars are.
exoplanet: A planet that goes around a star other than the Sun.
rover: A wheeled robot vehicle, controlled from Earth, that drives around on the Moon or another planet to explore it.
taikonaut: The name for Chinese astronauts, from the Chinese word "taikong", which means "space".
methane: A gas we use on Earth for cooking and heating. On Titan, it is so cold that methane is liquid and forms rivers and lakes.
radioactive: Describes a material that gives off heat and invisible rays. Kept safely shielded, it can supply energy for years.
comet: A chunk of ice and dust that travels around the Sun. As it gets close, it grows a glowing cloud and a long bright tail.
dwarf planet: A round world that goes around the Sun but isn't big enough to have "cleared" its path of other objects. Pluto is one.
reusable: Able to be used more than once. A reusable rocket comes back to Earth to be launched again.
infrared: A light our eyes can't see, linked to heat. Some cameras and telescopes can see it.
water ice: Frozen water. On the Moon or Mars, it could be used for drinking, breathing and making fuel.
radiation: Invisible, very energetic rays from the Sun and stars. In large amounts they are dangerous to health.
space debris: The junk circling the Earth: old satellites, pieces of rockets, fragments. It moves very fast and can damage spacecraft.
